speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Good morning everyone, welcome back to Learning Sciences, lecture four.

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Today is about one question: what actually happens in your brain when you learn something?

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: The short answer is neuroplasticity: the brain physically rewires itself every time you practise.

speaker: Jade
text: So the brain is not fixed after childhood?

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Not at all. Connections keep changing your whole life, just a bit slower as you age.

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Every connection between two neurons is called a synapse, and learning makes the useful ones stronger.

speaker: Leo
text: How does a synapse actually get stronger?

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Through long-term potentiation: when two neurons fire together again and again, the link between them grows.

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: That's where the classic phrase comes from: neurons that fire together, wire together.

speaker: Jade
text: And where are new memories stored at first?

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: In the hippocampus, a small curved structure deep inside each side of the brain.

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Think of it as a notebook: it writes things down quickly, but it can't keep them for long.

speaker: Leo
text: So what moves them out of the notebook?

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Mostly sleep. During memory consolidation the brain replays the day and copies the important parts to the cortex.

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: A lot of that replay happens in deep sleep, and REM sleep seems to help connect new ideas to old ones.

speaker: Jade
text: That explains why all-nighters before exams never work for me.

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Exactly. Without sleep you mostly lose what you crammed.

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: {listener}, what do you think happens to a memory if you sleep less than six hours after studying?

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Good guess. Studies show people remember up to forty percent less.

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Now, your brain can only juggle a few things at once. That limit is your working memory.

speaker: Leo
text: How many things can it hold?

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: About four chunks of information at a time, which is why long slides with ten bullet points don't stick.

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: When working memory is overloaded, we call it high cognitive load, and learning almost stops.

speaker: Jade
text: So what's the best way to study, then?

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Two techniques beat everything else. The first one is retrieval practice.

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Instead of rereading your notes, you close the book and try to recall the answer from memory.

speaker: Leo
text: Like flashcards?

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Yes, flashcards are a great example. The struggle to remember is what makes the memory stronger.

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: The second technique is spaced repetition: you review the same thing after one day, then three days, then a week.

speaker: Jade
text: Why does waiting longer help?

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Because you are about to forget. Each review flattens what Ebbinghaus called the forgetting curve.

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Motivation matters too. Dopamine is released when you expect a reward, and it helps you remember what you were doing.

speaker: Leo
text: Is that why games are so easy to remember?

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Partly, yes. Small wins keep the motivation going.

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Last point: stress. A little cortisol sharpens attention, but too much for too long damages the hippocampus.

speaker: Jade
text: So exam stress is actually bad for memory?

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Chronic stress is. One stressful morning is fine.

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: {listener}, could you sum up for everyone the two study techniques we covered today?

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: Perfect: retrieval practice and spaced repetition. Use both before the midterm.

speaker: Prof. Martin
text: For next week, read chapter five on attention. See you on Thursday.
